rows.a:
Deferral is the founding act of the human in Center Study. On the originary scene, a group converging on a shared object of desire is about to collapse into violence. Someone's grasping hand slows, others imitate it, and the reach becomes a gesture of aborted appropriation: the first sign. That conversion of grasping into pointing is deferral. It does not cancel the desire. It holds the violent convergence off, and the space this opens becomes the scene, with the object now sacred at its center.

Katz insists on the word because its near-synonyms ("postpone," "prevent," "refrain from") all imply a finished decision made from outside the situation. "If you’re deferring, you’re too much in the midst of things to make such a clear-cut distinction" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-2)). So deferral keeps us inside the scene, and it is never complete: "“deferral” posits no endpoint. As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). We also can't know exactly what we deferred: "no one could know that violence has been deferred, because no one can know what would have happened without the sign of deferral" ([Lecture 3](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-8)).

Deferral is also different from deterrence, where rivals simply watch each other. Deferral adds "a critical component: allowing for an orderly distribution" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). The object can be shared because everyone holds back together. That is why Katz can trace ritual, law, money and succession as layered institutions of deferral. A rushed "excuse me" in a crowd is a tiny instance of the same thing. It is also why deferral is not mainly about going without. Its effect "is not an intolerable feeling of privation… rather, the effect is of a new world opening up" ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-1)). Rivals can become collaborators, and a fight can turn into a joke.

To read next, start with [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence). It is short, and it shows why Katz thinks deferral keeps us still on the originary scene today.

rows.q: Why does Katz say there is no economy?
rows.a:
Katz's claim is that the "economy" is not a self-standing sphere of individuals freely trading, with politics and religion layered on top. What we call economic life is a late, partial form of something older: distribution from the center. In his words, "There is no “economy.” There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)).

This follows from the originary scene. The first thing shared was the central object, which "gives itself up" to be divided. Everything the community receives is therefore a gift from the center, and humans stand in an originary debt to it. Later forms repeat this structure: the sacrificial portion returned at the altar, the Big Man's distribution, the king's grants of land, coinage issued to pay soldiers. Markets do not arise spontaneously out of barter. They are delegated spaces: "Markets represent forms of delegation by the central authority—markets are areas of social life that are not under direct sovereign supervision" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-17)). Money, likewise, marks layers of distance from the center and the debts owed to it.

So "the economy" is better described as a ranking of positions within that distribution: "The “economy” is just everyone’s place, and everyone’s seeking to (re)place, in the order of having distributed to one and that one distributing to others" ([The Transfer Idiom](/post/the-transfer-idiom#p-11)). The liberal picture of self-interested exchange hides this dependence. It hides the fact that prices, property and credit all rest on someone keeping order and settling disputes.

Katz names the alternative a "tributary" order, in which the debt to the center is acknowledged openly rather than laundered through markets and central banks. In such an order, emulation rather than self-interest drives activity ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-95)).

Read next: that same essay, co-written with Zack Baker, [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf). It traces the argument from ritual through the founding of the Bank of England to derivatives.

rows.a:
For Katz, an idiom is any way of using language that takes its meaning from its own particular uses rather than from some higher, official vocabulary that would fix what words "really" mean. In his words, an idiom "is a singular use of language, meaningful in its particular and always changing uses" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-7)). The term is chosen against a target. "The reason for speaking of 'idioms' is to take any privileged metalanguage off the table, metalanguage being that bludgeon of the disciplines" ([Idiomatic Intelligence as Register](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-as-register#p-14)). Words like "cognition" or "belief" claim to stand above ordinary speech and define it from outside. To call everything an idiom refuses that claim. Katz pushes the point all the way: "There is nothing in language but idioms."

He borrows the word from Lyotard ([Idiom and the differend](/post/idiom-and-the-differend#p-6)), but gives it a grammatical content of his own. "An idiom is particular set of ostensive-imperative-interrogative-declarative sequences, so learning an idiom is learning when, for example, someone asking a question or making a statement is really requesting that you do something" ([Scenic/Event Intelligence](/post/scenic-event-intelligence#p-13)). Those are the basic speech forms of Center Study: pointing, commanding, asking, stating. To know an idiom is to know how a particular community or discipline links them. In one office "Have you finished the report?" is a question. In another it is an order.

How do idioms form? Think of a conversation that keeps itself going by reusing earlier words until they become shared reference points. Katz describes this as "the perpetual recycling of words used earlier so as to turn them into reference points that can frame the conversation itself. An idiom is that, sustained indefinitely" ([Programming the Same](/post/programming-the-same#p-27)). Every idiom is a small iteration of the originary scene, a way of getting people to point together at something and say "this is the same." That is why Katz can call the originary hypothesis "the idiomaticity of idioms." The practical task he sets is to move across idioms and translate between them, and also to coin new ones, without retreating to a master language above them all.

To read next, try [Idiomatic Intelligence as Register](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-as-register). It shows how working inside idioms becomes a way of gathering intelligence about the scenes we are on.

rows.a:
The Big Man is the figure who first puts a human being at the center of the community. Katz takes the term from the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins by way of Eric Gans, who saw it as perhaps the most revolutionary event in human history after the originary scene itself. In the earliest communities the center was held by the shared object of ritual, an animal or ancestor, and distribution followed ritual rules. The Big Man breaks that order through discipline and generosity: "The Big Man, in archaic social orders, becomes big by out-gifting his competitors" ([Discipline and Debt](/post/discipline-and-debt#p-1)). Once everyone owes him more than they could ever repay, he no longer takes part in the exchange of gifts. He becomes the source of distribution.

That is why Katz treats him as the origin of hierarchy and of politics. "The emergence of the Big Man destroys, once and for all, the egalitarianism of the primitive community." It also changes the kind of resentment people feel: the Big Man "doesn't just have things that others want but sets the terms of communal interactions" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-5)). His position is precarious. Rivals want it, and his ability to provide can fail. The lines of sacral kingship and then divine empire develop out of efforts to make that occupancy secure. As Katz puts it, "Once the center has been humanly occupied, it must remain humanly occupied" ([Sacral Kingship and After](/post/sacral-kingship-and-after-preliminary-reflections#p-2)).

Here Katz departs from Gans. Gans set out the concept and then, in Katz's words, "did nothing with it." Katz builds his political thought around it. He traces a line "from the Big Man, to the chief, to the sacred king, to the divine emperor" ([Downstream of the Imperative](/post/downstream-of-the-imperative#p-9)), and from there to every presidency and every boss. He also defends what he calls the "Big Man revolution" against attempts to restore an imagined egalitarian order. On this view the central political question is never whether someone occupies the center. It is how they occupy it, and how the center passes to the next occupant.

To read next, [Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction) is short and lays out the problems the Big Man must solve: rivals, disputes among his subjects, and resentment. It then follows these problems into the question of secure sovereignty.

rows.a:
No, but Katz admits the question is a fair one. Center Study grows out of the originary hypothesis: language, the human and the sacred begin together in one event, a gesture around a shared center that defers violence. A theory of where the sacred comes from will look a lot like a religion. Katz says GA (Gans's Generative Anthropology, which Center Study extends) is "very similar to a religion and at the same time the exact opposite of one" ([The Originary Hypothesis in Itself](/post/the-originary-hypothesis-in-itself#p-4)). It is "the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)).

The difference is in where it starts. It does not ask you to believe in a God. It offers a hypothesis about how any God, rite or sacred name could arise. Even so, Katz sides with faith against philosophy and secular debunking: "the faiths are truer than philosophy, and it's not even close" ([same, p-2](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)). The divine drops out as an object of belief, but what replaces it still governs: "the center which can never quite be 'human' yet governs all" ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-5)).

Katz goes further than that. He calls "spirituality," "religion" and "faith" "hypotheses I consider defunct" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-12)). He does not mean the sacred is unreal. He means everything those words point to is better understood through language. In one essay he goes as far as "Language, then, is fundamentally prayer" ([Mobius Strip, p-10](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-10)). He imagines religions treated this way becoming "a kind of center study" themselves, each competing to show the best way of deferring violence ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-21)). So Center Study is neither a faith nor a secular alternative to faith. It is a way of studying, and taking part in, what faiths do.

Read [Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip) next. It is Katz's most direct treatment of why the hypothesis sits "closest and furthest from any faith tradition," and of what that asks of the person who takes it up.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
Center Study would read a pile-on as violent centralization in miniature: attention converging on one figure, with each new contribution prompted less by the target than by the people already contributing. Katz uses exactly this example. On the urge to add your own jab, he writes: "There is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple" ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1)). From there he gets his minimal definition: "The center is whatever interferes with violent centralization." A pile-on is the opposite of that. It is the rush to the center on the originary scene, the gathering around a shared object, without the gesture of deferral that holds everyone back from seizing it.

Katz also locates the pile-on in the media scene rather than in individual psychology. Modern media, in his account, stage endless trials. The result is "each individual being placed with ever greater regularity and urgency on perpetual 'call' to add one's own voice in judgment to the crowd directed at the target of the day" ([Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation#p-10)). Every pile-on also carries an implicit claim about power: "The claim implicit in scapegoating is that the center has been usurped by someone 'behind the scenes'" ([Bouvard on Scapegoating](/post/the-egalitarian-vs-hierarchical-model-of-morality#p-1)). The target is treated as an illegitimate occupant of the center, and the crowd as its rightful avenger.

Center Study's answer is not to pile on the pilers, which would only repeat the pattern. It asks a design question instead. Katz holds that "the nature of social media is more to be used to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger" ([Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14)). He doesn't rule out criticism or judgment; condemnation and punishment remain legitimate. The open question he presses is where the boundary lies between judging someone and joining a convergence on them.

To read next: [Media as Infrastructural Translation](/post/media-as-infrastructural-translation). It explains why our media keep producing these scenes of vicarious judgment, and it sketches what an order built around succession rather than spectacle might look like.
